summary: Defines how a recipient can pull a series of Security Event Tokens (SETs) from a sender by polling with HTTP POST over TLS. This is the counterpart to push delivery: the recipient asks when it is ready, and the protocol also describes how to acknowledge events so delivery can be assured.

eli5.summary: Instead of waiting for the mail carrier, you walk to the mailbox yourself every so often, take out new letters, and tell the sender which ones you got.

subtitle: How a receiver pulls security events from a sender by polling with HTTP POST, and tells the sender which ones arrived.

tldr.problem: Some receivers of Security Event Tokens (SETs) can make outbound HTTP requests but cannot host an endpoint the sender can reach, so push delivery does not fit.
tldr.mechanism: The SET Recipient sends HTTP POST polls to an endpoint the SET Transmitter hosts. Each poll can carry acknowledgements (ack) and error reports (setErrs) for earlier SETs, and the response returns a batch of SETs keyed by their jti.
tldr.outcome: Acknowledged SETs release the transmitter from keeping them, which gives assured delivery as far as the recipient needs it. This is the counterpart to push delivery in RFC 8935.

today: RFC 8936 is a Proposed Standard published in November 2020. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its push-based counterpart is RFC 8935.

sections.title: Polling for Security Events
sections.content:
RFC 8936 defines how a stream of Security Event Tokens (SETs, from RFC 8417) can be sent to a SET Recipient over HTTP and TLS when the recipient starts each exchange by polling with HTTP POST. It is the alternative to the push method in RFC 8935.

Poll delivery suits cases where the recipient can make outbound HTTP requests, the transmitter can host a TLS-enabled HTTP endpoint the recipient can reach, and both sides are willing to exchange data. Exchanging configuration such as endpoint URLs, keys and buffer limits is out of scope.
sections.eli5: Polling is for when you can walk to the mailbox but the sender cannot walk to your door. You go and check it.

sections.title: How Polling Delivery Works
sections.content:
When a SET is ready, the transmitter queues it in a buffer. The recipient polls with an HTTP POST and receives zero or more SETs in a JSON document. In its next request it acknowledges what it received and can ask for more. All requests and responses are JSON documents with Content-Type: application/json.

Polling can be periodic (short polling) or the request can wait until a new SET is available (long polling, per RFC 6202). Short polling returns zero or more SETs; long polling typically returns one or more unless it times out.

Once a SET is acknowledged, the transmitter need not keep it for retransmission and the recipient becomes responsible for retention. The transmitter may also discard undelivered SETs under deployment-specific conditions, such as not being polled for too long. The recipient validates each SET as described in RFC 8935 and MUST acknowledge receipt, in a timely way. It SHALL NOT use acknowledgement to report errors other than those about parsing and validating the SET.
sections.eli5: The sender keeps letters in a pile. You come and take some, and next time you visit you say which ones you got, so they can throw those copies away.

sections.title: Poll Requests and Responses
sections.content:
A poll request is a JSON object. Processing members: maxEvents (optional integer, the most unacknowledged SETs to return; 0 means an acknowledge-only request; omitted means no limit) and returnImmediately (optional boolean; true asks for short polling, and the default false means long polling). Acknowledgement members: ack, an array of the jti values of SETs received successfully, and setErrs, an object keyed by the jti of invalid SETs whose values give an err and a description. Either may be omitted when empty.

The response is a JSON object with sets, an object whose member names are the jti of each SET and whose values are the SET strings (empty if nothing is waiting), and moreAvailable, a boolean saying whether more unacknowledged SETs remain (omitting it means false). SETs sent for the first time and SETs resent because they were not acknowledged both appear in sets.
sections.eli5: You hand over a slip saying how many letters you can carry and whether to wait. They hand back a bundle, each letter tagged with its own number, and tell you if there are more.

sections.title: The Three Kinds of Poll
sections.content:
A poll request comes in three variations. A poll-only request has no ack or setErrs, as in the first poll, and a recipient can poll with an empty JSON object {} to use all defaults. An acknowledge-only request sets maxEvents to 0 along with ack and setErrs; if it must return at once, returnImmediately MUST be true, otherwise a long poll still waits for an event even though none will be returned. A combined request acknowledges earlier SETs and waits for the next group in one call.

When some SETs were invalid, the recipient MAY report them in setErrs while listing good ones in ack. Error values come from the IANA Security Event Token Error Codes registry set up by RFC 8935, and a request containing errors MUST carry a Content-Language header.

After a period configured out of band, a transmitter MAY redeliver SETs and MAY limit how many times it tries. The recipient SHOULD accept repeats and acknowledge them anyway, and SHOULD acknowledge within seconds or minutes, before acting on the SETs.
sections.eli5: You can just ask for letters, just say "I got these", or do both at once. If a letter was torn or fake, you say so by its number.

sections.title: Poll Responses and Errors
sections.content:
If SETs are available the transmitter MAY answer at once. If none are and returnImmediately is not true, it SHALL delay the response until a SET is ready or the timeout elapses; the timeout is part of the out-of-band configuration. A response with no SETs contains "sets": {}.

For a general HTTP problem the service provider returns the applicable status code. It MAY use 400 (Bad Request) for any invalid poll request, even when a more specific code exists, for example to avoid disclosing information, and SHALL use 400 when no more specific code applies. The body of such a response is undefined and SHOULD be ignored.
sections.eli5: If there is nothing yet, the sender waits until a letter arrives, unless you said "just tell me now". If your slip was broken they simply say "bad request".

sections.title: Authentication, Security and Privacy
sections.content:
As in push delivery, this method relies on HTTP over TLS and standard HTTP authentication. The TLS server certificate MUST be validated using DNS-ID and/or DANE, and a delivery endpoint SHALL list the supported schemes in WWW-Authenticate when using HTTP authentication. After acknowledging a SET, a recipient is free to ignore it, because SETs are not commands.

SETs may hold personal data, so confidentiality MUST be protected. The endpoint MUST support at least TLS 1.2 and SHOULD support the newest suitable version, named in the text as TLS 1.3. RFC 7525 MUST be followed, and some uses also need JWE encryption.

If OAuth access tokens are used, the threats in Section 8 of RFC 7521 MUST be considered. Bearer tokens (RFC 6750) should travel over TLS and SHOULD have a limited lifetime; the text notes that a client MAY use an OAuth refresh token to get a new one. Implementers are encouraged to prefer authentication stronger than HTTP Basic (RFC 7617). The privacy rules match RFC 8935: obtain legal agreements and user consent before sharing personal information, and think about whether subject identifiers are sensitive.
sections.eli5: Everything goes in a locked tube, and the keys you show at the door should expire so a stolen key stops working.
